articles.title: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Cluster: 6.3GW Power and Water Supply Key to 2030 Mass Production - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Cluster: 6.3GW Power and Water Supply Key to 2030 Mass Production  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are accelerating the Honam Semiconductor Cluster, a project with total investment exceeding 800 trillion won (approximately $595.8 billion), targeting first mass production by 2030. Whether power and water infrastructure can be secured in time has emerged as the key variable determining the project's success or failure.
Around 20 officials from the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City's semiconductor industry support division and related bureaus visited Samsung Electronics' Pyeongtaek Campus on the 6th. This marks their second visit, following one on July 29. The delegation toured fabs and utility facilities within the Pyeongtaek Campus to examine semiconductor production processes and power and water supply systems, and planned to hear investment-related opinions and recommendations from Samsung Electronics.
They subsequently visited Pyeongtaek City Hall to review the administrative framework that simultaneously supports land, power, water, transportation, and logistics required for semiconductor plants. In the afternoon, they toured the Godeok International New Town and Brain City to inspect residential hinterland and commuting conditions.
The Pyeongtaek Campus currently operates four fabs, with a fifth fab, P5, under construction. Samsung Electronics is rushing to expand Pyeongtaek in response to growing demand for AI memory while simultaneously investing in the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex. The integrated city's return visit to Pyeongtaek is aimed at directly observing how a region already equipped with large-scale production facilities and infrastructure operates.
2030 Mass Production Target: Power and Water Are the Key
The Honam Semiconductor Cluster is a project to build a production hub of four fabs on the former Gwangju Military Airport site, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix investing a combined total of over 800 trillion won. The Korea Land & Housing Corporation (LH) is currently conducting survey and design services for the national industrial complex. The total site spans approximately 2.5 million pyeong, with plans to prioritize development of approximately 630,000 pyeong.
The South Korean government and the integrated city aim to begin groundwork on the priority development site as early as next year and commence first mass production by mid-2030. Discussions with SK Hynix are ongoing. The integrated city plans to sign a move-in agreement with SK Hynix this month, followed by negotiations on detailed investment conditions including land, construction, power, and water.
To meet the 2030 mass production target, power and water supply networks must be established before fab construction. Full operation of four fabs is estimated to require approximately 6.3 gigawatts (GW) of power. Initially, existing substations and power grids will be utilized, with plans to add transmission lines and substation facilities as production capacity expands.
Industrial water demand is projected at up to 650,000 tons per day. Semiconductor production requires massive volumes of ultrapure water for wafer cleaning and other processes, meaning water source development and pipeline construction must align with fab operation timelines.
The integrated city's plan calls for supplying an initial 3.1GW of power, scaling up to approximately 6.3GW as production facilities expand, and securing 150,000 tons of daily water supply by the end of 2028 before expanding supply capacity in phases.
The following table summarizes the core infrastructure demand and supply plans for the Honam cluster:
| Category | Final Demand | Initial Supply Target | Notes | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Power | Approx. 6.3GW | 3.1GW | Phased expansion aligned with production facility growth | 
| Industrial Water | Up to 650,000 tons/day | 150,000 tons/day by end of 2028 | Water source development and pipeline construction in parallel | 
In August, the South Korean government pushed for exemptions from preliminary feasibility studies for related projects to accelerate power and water infrastructure development for the Honam Semiconductor Cluster. The Korea Semiconductor Industry Association also stated in a position paper on August 11 regarding the implementation of the Special Semiconductor Act: "It is of paramount importance that investment support, core infrastructure development including power and water, and follow-up support policies are pursued swiftly and consistently."
Comparison with Pyeongtaek and Yongin: Infrastructure Determines Operational Timing
In Pyeongtaek and Yongin as well, power and water are the critical conditions determining fab operational timing. Pyeongtaek already has transmission networks, water pipelines, roads, and a supplier base in place, enabling Samsung Electronics to rapidly proceed with follow-up investments such as P5.
By contrast, the Yongin Idong-Namsa National Industrial Complex, where Samsung Electronics will be located, requires not only land compensation and site preparation but also simultaneous construction of transmission and water networks. Even if production facility construction proceeds quickly, actual operational timing can be delayed if infrastructure lags behind.
SK Hynix is likewise building its first fab at the Yongin Wonsam-myeon semiconductor cluster while continuing investments in its Cheongju production facilities. Once Honam investment begins in earnest, the company will be undertaking large-scale investments simultaneously in Yongin, Cheongju, and Honam.
Industry observers view the ability to supply power and water when actually needed as the more critical factor for the Honam cluster. With demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI growing rapidly, any misalignment between production facility and infrastructure construction schedules could delay mass production timing.
Combining Gwangju's Land with Jeonnam's Infrastructure
The Honam Semiconductor Cluster is a project that combines Gwangju's industrial base and land with Jeonnam's power, water, and renewable energy infrastructure resources. Before integration, Gwangju's industrial land and corporate support policies and Jeonnam's power generation facilities, water resources, and renewable energy had to be coordinated between separate local governments. Now, a single integrated city can bundle these elements and present them as investment conditions to companies while coordinating the project.
The integrated city is not limiting its ambitions to attracting semiconductor plants. It plans to expand into AI, renewable energy, data centers, and materials, components, and equipment industries, linking the South Korean government's maximum integrated support of 20 trillion won (approximately $14.9 billion) and the second phase of public institution relocation to build a super-regional industrial ecosystem.
On the fiscal front, the integrated city has decided to allocate 6 trillion won (approximately $4.5 billion) of the maximum 20 trillion won in fiscal incentives secured through integration toward semiconductor infrastructure, forward and backward industrial ecosystems, and specialized workforce development from 2027 to 2030.
Semiconductor investment has also provided new momentum for the long-stalled relocation of Gwangju Military Airport. Since the military airport site must be vacated for semiconductor production facilities to be built on schedule, the airport relocation has become linked to national advanced industry investment timelines, transcending its status as a long-standing regional issue. The South Korean government is also pursuing temporary dispersal of military functions and relocation procedures in parallel with fab groundbreaking.
Plans are also underway to attract materials, components, and equipment companies centered on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and to connect Gwangju's existing back-end processing base, including Amkor Technology Korea, to concentrate the semiconductor forward and backward industries in the region. By linking the national AI computing center at Haenam Solar City, private data centers, and Jeonnam's renewable energy production base, the project could expand into a super-regional industrial axis spanning semiconductor production, back-end processing, AI, and energy.
However, challenges remain: the industrial complex development, military airport relocation, and power and water supply networks must all be built on schedules aligned with corporate timelines, and the benefits of semiconductor investment must be spread beyond the Gwangju Military Airport area to industries and jobs across the entire Jeonnam-Gwangju region.

articles.title: Analysis: China's five strategic objectives for the Korean Peninsula - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Analysis: China's five strategic objectives for the Korean Peninsula  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's visit to South Korea in August 2026, while receiving relatively muted international coverage compared to higher-profile diplomatic summits, represented a consequential articulation of Beijing's strategic calculus for the Korean Peninsula. Meeting with South Korean national security advisors in Seoul, Wang delivered China's foreign policy objectives with unusual candor, outlining a comprehensive framework designed to manage North Korean belligerence, constrain United States military influence, and preserve regional stability in a manner conducive to China's broader geopolitical interests.
Managing North Korean Belligerence and Denuclearization
At the core of China's strategy is the maintenance of permanent peace and stability on the peninsula, which Beijing views as essential for its own economic development and border security. While China remains North Korea's primary economic lifeline and diplomatic shield, Wang's visit underscored Beijing's categorical rejection of Pyongyang's nuclear weapons program. Chinese scholars and policymakers increasingly view North Korea's missile launches and nuclear development not merely as a threat to regional security, but as a catalyst for the very security architecture Beijing opposes: a consolidated United States-South Korea-Japan military alliance.
To manage this dilemma, China has adopted a strategy of conditional engagement. Beijing leverages North Korea's economic dependence to extract specific acts of restraint, conditioning humanitarian assistance, border trade access, and energy supplies on Pyongyang's willingness to avoid military escalation. This approach reflects a pragmatic recognition that while China cannot dictate North Korean policy, it can impose tangible costs on belligerent behavior that threatens to trigger expanded US military deployments in Northeast Asia.
Opposing Bloc Politics and Security Integration
A central theme of Wang's diplomatic outreach was China's firm opposition to the emergence of competing security blocs in the region. Beijing is deeply concerned by the strengthening ties between Russia and North Korea, fearing that a formalized Moscow-Pyongyang alignment could provide a pretext for Japan, South Korea, and the United States to accelerate their own trilateral security integration. For China, the biggest risk of closer North Korean-Russian cooperation is that it hardens the region into a Cold War-style bipolar architecture, limiting Beijing's strategic flexibility and increasing the likelihood of accidental escalation.
Consequently, China is actively encouraging South Korea to preserve its strategic autonomy. By offering Seoul enhanced economic cooperation, particularly in high-technology sectors, artificial intelligence, and the silver economy, Beijing seeks to provide a compelling alternative to deeper integration with the US-led security apparatus. The message to South Korean policymakers is clear: Seoul's long-term prosperity and security are better served by maintaining a balanced relationship with its largest trading partner, rather than subordinating its foreign policy to Washington's strategic competition with China.
Reducing US Military Influence and the Taiwan Nexus
Beyond the immediate dynamics of the Korean Peninsula, China's strategy is inextricably linked to its broader objectives regarding the United States and Taiwan. Beijing's concept of denuclearization applies to the entire peninsula, encompassing not only the dismantlement of North Korea's nuclear arsenal but also the reduction of US extended nuclear deterrence and the withdrawal of American ground troops. From the Chinese perspective, the heavy US military footprint in South Korea is a legacy of the Cold War that sustains a regional security dilemma and limits China's ability to project power in its near abroad.
Furthermore, preventing the consolidation of a hostile US-ROK-Japan security bloc is critical to China's strategy for the Taiwan Strait. A unified, heavily armed trilateral alliance in Northeast Asia would reinforce a regional security architecture that Beijing regards as increasingly directed against its core interests. By keeping South Korea strategically autonomous and resistant to full integration into a US-led containment strategy, China aims to limit the strategic pressure on its eastern flank, preserving the diplomatic and military bandwidth necessary to manage the Taiwan issue on its own terms.
The Pursuit of Strategic Equilibrium
Ultimately, Wang Yi's visit highlighted China's pursuit of a new strategic equilibrium in Northeast Asia. Beijing accepts that the United States will remain its principal competitor, but it seeks to define the boundaries of that competition, insisting on cooperation where interests align while firmly resisting what it perceives as containment. China's strategy on the Korean Peninsula is therefore not merely reactive; it is an active, multi-vector effort to shape the choices of Seoul, Pyongyang, and Washington.
By wielding its economic leverage over the North, offering market access to the South, and articulating a vision of regional security that excludes external military blocs, China is attempting to engineer a stable periphery that supports its long-term rise. The success of this audacious initiative will depend on whether South Korea is willing to resist the gravitational pull of the US alliance system, and whether North Korea can be persuaded that restraint yields greater dividends than provocation.

articles.summary: Research institutions warn that allowing China to export advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment will result in a loss of its competitive advantage in the AI field.  GIGAZINE
articles.full_text:
The Center for Technology & Statecraft, a US-based AI and semiconductor policy research institute, has published a report stating that if the US allows the export of advanced semiconductor lithography equipment, essential for AI chip manufacturing, to China, it will lose its competitive edge within the next 5 to 10 years. The report also recommends countermeasures, as some advanced lithography equipment is already being exported through loopholes.
DUV Immersion Lithography: The Foundation of the US AI Advantage - Center for Technology & Statecraft
https://techstatecraft.org/duv/
When considering the production of competitive AI chips, advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment is essential. According to a report by the Technology & Statecraft Center, China is unlikely to be able to mass-produce such equipment even in the mid-2030s, allowing the United States and its allies to maintain an advantage.
However, the Trump administration has announced a policy to allow China to import deep ultraviolet immersion (DUVi) semiconductor lithography equipment capable of manufacturing advanced AI chips. While exports of less advanced DUVi equipment have been permitted in the past, the report warns that if exports of advanced DUVi equipment continue at the same pace, China will acquire sufficient semiconductor manufacturing capabilities within the next 5 to 10 years, diminishing or eliminating the advantage held by the United States and its allies in the field of AI chips.
The Technology & Statecraft Center suggests that 'these results can be prevented with simple policy changes.'
First, we must 'ban the export of DUVi to China.' The graph on the left shows the scenario if China maintains its DUVi imports, where China's AI chip production (shown in red) is expected to rapidly approach that of the United States (shown in blue). On the other hand, the graph on the right shows the scenario if China's DUVi imports are prevented, where China's AI chip production will not reach that of the United States.
The current standard has been to regulate extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment, especially highly advanced DUVi systems, which are essential for manufacturing high-performance chips. Some highly advanced DUVi systems are licensed, while less advanced DUVi systems and dry DUV systems can be exported without a license. However, the Technology & Statecraft Center is advocating for a complete export ban, with the exception of dry DUV systems.
In practice, this 'licensing method' is largely permitted, and it appears that China has acquired a total of 300 DUVi units, primarily 
The current number of lithography machines does not pose a threat to the United States, but the Technology & Statecraft Center points out that if China were to acquire NXT:1980i and similar DUVi machines at a similar pace and fully engage in AI chip production, it could produce hundreds of millions of H100 equivalent chips.
The Technology & Statecraft Centre suggests that if the Netherlands and Japan remain passive in closing the loopholes China uses to acquire DUVi, they could impose export restrictions using the Foreign Direct Products Rule (FDPR) or shut down ASML factories that use American tools using export control regulations.
Furthermore, it was reported in July 2026 that a Chinese state-owned enterprise had begun manufacturing DUV lithography equipment.

articles.summary: Japanese Yen softens as BoJ rate hike expectations recede, FOMC Minutes loom  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The USD/JPY pair gathers strength to around 158.35 during the early Asian trading hours on Wednesday. Receding expectations for a rate hike by the Bank of Japan (BoJ) weigh on the Japanese Yen (JPY) against the US Dollar (USD). Traders will closely monitor the Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) later on Wednesday.
BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Tuesday that the central bank would "assess the likelihood and risks of the baseline economic and price outlook being realized" when considering the pace and timing of future rate hikes. Market views that the Japanese central bank would take a cautious stance on rate increase at its October monetary policy meeting, weighing on the JPY.
The Bank of Japan's (BoJ) new policymaker Ayano Sato said that she supports the idea of raising interest rates in several stages, Reuters reported on Tuesday.
Pricing in overnight index swaps implies that markets see around a 12% odds of a rate hike this month, down from as high as 40% early last week, according to Bloombegr. The current probability surge to around 90% when the December meeting is included.
On the US’s front, traders reduce their bets on a Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike this month following the softer-than-expected US jobs data. The US Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) rose by 29K in September, compared to the 133K increase seen in August, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) showed on Friday. This figure came in below the market consensus of 90K. The Unemployment Rate climbed to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.
BoJ rate path seen as gradual as Fed tightening bets support elevated USD/JPY
Analysts at Rabobank note that, following the “as expected 25 bps rate rise last month,” market pricing now “suggests only a limited prospect of a policy move at the October 30 meeting, with expectations centring on December for the next policy move.” Even though BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated this morning that policymakers intend to “continue raising the policy interest rate” and described the Japanese economy as growing “moderately,” Rabobank argues that “this strengthens the market’s expectation that back-to-back rate hikes BoJ are unlikely.” As they put it, “even so, the Bank is still not widely viewed as being in a position in which back-to-back rate rises are appropriate,” although “this may suggest that a hastened pace of rate hikes is possible, though clearly that depends on how the economy develops in the months ahead.”
On the external side, Rabobank’s house view is that “the market has anticipated too much Fed policy tightening next year.” They contend that, “assuming some Fed rate hike risk is priced out, USD/JPY has the potential to move lower into 2027,” but for now “we maintain a 3-month USD/JPY target of 155.00.” While USD/JPY has moved higher since the September policy meeting, Rabobank highlights that “the market is fearful that a return to levels close to 160, could again trigger further intervention.” Against this backdrop, they judge that the BoJ’s inflation objective “now appears to have reached the point when it can instead shift its focus to stabilising price pressures around the target level,” reinforcing expectations for a measured, rather than aggressive, tightening path.
Fed’s schmid flags ai-driven inflation, keeps fed credibility and short-rate path in focus
Fed’s Schmid delivers a distinctly hawkish tone, with an 8/10 FXS Speechtracker score modestly above the 7.5/10 historical average, underscoring a firmer stance relative to the established baseline. The emphasis that inflation is “frustrating,” that the Fed “still has a way to go,” and that AI is now “one of the largest drivers of inflation” highlights concern about persistent price pressures and emerging structural forces, while the assertion that Fed credibility is at stake and that “the Fed still has work to do on the short rate despite higher long-term yields” signals a willingness to maintain or even tighten policy despite the bond market backdrop.
The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rose by 0.34 points to 137.91, reinforcing that the broader policy tone remains firmly in hawkish territory well above the neutral 100 threshold. This incremental uptick, aligned with the stronger-than-baseline speech score, suggests that Fed communication continues to support a resilient Dollar bias as markets price in a prolonged restrictive stance.
Technical Analysis: USD/JPY keeps a bearish vibe below the 100-day SMA
In the daily chart, USD/JPY remains capped in the near term, with the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and the upper Bollinger Band forming overhead resistance that restrains recovery attempts. Price holds above the middle Bollinger Band, while the 14-day Relative Strength Index at 56.27 shows moderately constructive momentum that has yet to overcome the prevailing bearish structural bias set by the dominant longer-term average.
On the topside, initial resistance is located at the 100-day SMA at 159.55, followed by the upper Bollinger Band near 159.80. On the downside, immediate support sits at the middle Bollinger Band at 156.90, with a deeper cushion at the lower Bollinger Band around 154.00 should selling pressure reassert below the recent pivot at 158.38.

Japanese Yen FAQs
The Japanese Yen (JPY) is one of the world’s most traded currencies. Its value is broadly determined by the performance of the Japanese economy, but more specifically by the Bank of Japan’s policy, the differential between Japanese and US bond yields, or risk sentiment among traders, among other factors.
One of the Bank of Japan’s mandates is currency control, so its moves are key for the Yen. The BoJ has directly intervened in currency markets sometimes, generally to lower the value of the Yen, although it refrains from doing it often due to political concerns of its main trading partners. The BoJ ultra-loose monetary policy between 2013 and 2024 caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks. More recently, the gradually unwinding of this ultra-loose policy has given some support to the Yen.
Over the last decade, the BoJ’s stance of sticking to ultra-loose monetary policy has led to a widening policy divergence with other central banks, particularly with the US Federal Reserve. This supported a widening of the differential between the 10-year US and Japanese bonds, which favored the US Dollar against the Japanese Yen. The BoJ decision in 2024 to gradually abandon the ultra-loose policy, coupled with interest-rate cuts in other major central banks, is narrowing this differential.
The Japanese Yen is often seen as a safe-haven investment. This means that in times of market stress, investors are more likely to put their money in the Japanese currency due to its supposed reliability and stability. Turbulent times are likely to strengthen the Yen’s value against other currencies seen as more risky to invest in.

SK Hynix Semiconductors Also Board Nuri Rocket... Korean Companies Validate Technology in Space
Verifying DRAM and UFS Performance in Space
Rising Demand for High-Performance Semiconductors in the Space Environment
Expanding Space Industry: From Batteries to Industrial Gases
On October 7, domestic companies are targeting the space market through the fifth launch of the Korean launch vehicle Nuri rocket. They are testing the performance of semiconductors, batteries, and electronic components by loading them onto satellites, evaluating their function in the extreme environment of space. Companies are also participating in the manufacture of launch vehicles and the construction of ground infrastructure. Their strategy is to expand the technological expertise developed in their core businesses to the space sector, thereby securing new drivers of growth.
This launch will carry a record-high total of 15 satellites. Among these, SK hynix's DRAM and universal flash storage (UFS) will be loaded onto the second space verification satellite. This initiative is part of the "Domestic Devices and Components Space Verification Support Project," led by the Korea Aerospace Administration and the Korea Aerospace Research Institute. The goal is to test whether the memory operates normally in space and whether it can withstand radiation. Last year, during the fourth Nuri rocket launch, Samsung Electronics' DRAM and NAND flash memory were loaded onto the first space verification satellite.
The same satellite will also carry key components from domestic space companies, such as Inserasolutions' high-speed precision steering mirror and Momentum Space's reaction wheel. LG Group will load five types of parts from three of its affiliates, including camera modules and battery packs, onto a CubeSat and test their performance in orbit for about 60 days.
The Future Growth Engine Is Space: Korean Companies Enter Practical Demonstrations
SK hynix's DRAM and NAND heading to space aboard the Nuri rocket. Korea Aerospace Research Institute.
View original image
Companies are venturing into space validation to secure the reliability of their products in preparation for market expansion. With growing data needs, such as autonomous spacecraft operation and real-time video analysis on observation satellites, the potential use cases for advanced semiconductors are increasing. The World Economic Forum (WEF) and McKinsey forecast that the global space economy will reach 1.8 trillion dollars by 2035.
Memory companies, including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, are testing whether semiconductors can adapt to the space environment and are seeking to enter the space electronics equipment market. In April, the two companies supplied semiconductors for the Korean CubeSat “K-RadCube” aboard Artemis II. As global technology companies accelerate the build-out of space artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, Korean firms appear to be exploring opportunities for space exploration semiconductors. The amount of data requiring processing—from autonomous spacecraft navigation to real-time, high-resolution Earth observation satellite imagery—is surging, making the adoption of advanced semiconductors in the space and aerospace industry inevitable.
Electronics and component manufacturers have likewise begun pioneering new markets. LG Group, leveraging the outcomes of this demonstration, has set a target to launch its own CubeSat by 2028, expanding business opportunities in the space environment. The company plans to achieve results and generate revenue from its space operations by 2030.
POSCO is also extending its business scope into the aerospace sector. Last April, the company signed a business agreement with the Korea Aerospace Research Institute and is currently working on the development and localization of rare gas blending technologies—including xenon and krypton—for use as satellite propellants. Through the recently established POSCO Air Solution, POSCO intends to expand its business to include other industrial gases for aerospace applications, such as liquid oxygen, nitrogen, argon, and helium.
From Development to Launch: Building the Foundation for the Space Industry

Domestic companies are playing key roles in the production and launch infrastructure of the Nuri rocket. Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI) is in charge of the propellant tank production and overall system assembly for the fifth launch, as they were for the third and fourth launches. The company is responsible for fabricating the key launch vehicle components and integrating them into a complete launch vehicle.
HD Hyundai Heavy Industries was responsible for the ground infrastructure necessary to launch the rocket into space. Drawing on its experience building the launch pad for the Naro rocket (KSLV-I), the company secured a contract in 2016 from the Korea Aerospace Research Institute to build the Korean launch pad system and established the dedicated second launch pad for the Nuri rocket at the Naro Space Center. The company independently designed, manufactured, and installed the launch pad systems—including mechanical ground support equipment (MGSE), propellant ground support equipment (FGSE), and electrical ground support equipment (EGSE)—and is involved in launch operations. The company emphasizes that the localization rate for launch pad system process technology has reached 100%, ensuring that all launch infrastructure can now be built and operated with domestic technology. Ahead of the fifth Nuri launch, the company repaired key equipment and inspected system performance after the fourth launch.
Hyundai Rotem is responsible for the testing infrastructure that verifies propulsion system performance prior to each launch. The propulsion system test facilities at the Naro Space Center are used to test the propulsion systems and combustion performance of the first, second, and third stages of the Nuri rocket with flow and combustion tests. Design began in 2011, and development was completed in 2021. This facility has been used for every launch from the second through the fifth Nuri launches.

articles.title: [News] Micron’s Expansion Push Lifts Korean Chip Suppliers, with Hanmi’s HBM TC Bonder Reportedly in Focus - TrendForce
articles.summary: [News] Micron’s Expansion Push Lifts Korean Chip Suppliers, with Hanmi’s HBM TC Bonder Reportedly in Focus  TrendForce
articles.full_text:
Riding a memory-price rally and strong earnings, Micron is doubling down on expansion. MK Economy reports that the U.S. memory giant expects $25 billion in CapEx in 1HFY27—nearly matching its $27.37 billion full-year FY26 spending. Yet even as Micron closes in on Samsung and SK hynix, its expansion could spell a windfall for Korean chip suppliers including Hanmi Semiconductor, Justem and CMTX, according to Financial News.
Financial News suggests Hanmi Semiconductor is emerging as a key beneficiary of Micron’s growing presence in the memory market, with the company reportedly supplying thermal compression (TC) bonders and related equipment to the U.S. memory giant. As reported, TC bonders precisely stack and bond DRAM dies by applying controlled heat and pressure, making them essential equipment in the production of HBM.
Notably, the report points to strong ties between the two parties, as Hanmi Semiconductor was officially invited to and attended Micron’s semiconductor facility groundbreaking and completion ceremonies in Singapore and India in January and March, respectively. By year-end, the company plans to establish a U.S. subsidiary, Hanmi USA, in San Jose, California, strengthening local support for customers including Micron, the report adds.
That relationship could gain further momentum as Micron accelerates its HBM ramp. At its September 30 earnings call, Micron said HBM revenue grew faster than companywide revenue in fiscal Q4 2026 as shipments expanded across a broader customer base. Looking ahead, the company has already locked in agreements for the vast majority of its 2027 HBM bit supply at significantly higher prices than in 2026.
Justem, CMTX Poised to Benefit
On the other hand, Justem is also being cited as a potential beneficiary of Micron’s expansion. South Korea's government has announced a technology build-out that needs an extra 27.7 gigawatts (GW) of power by 2040, but has not decided whether to build more nuclear plants to supply it, according to the World Nuclear Industry Status Report 2026 (WNISR).
The "Three Major Megaprojects" plan, announced in June 2026 with Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and other companies, covers semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence (AI), and AI data centres.
Companies will invest a reported $3.2t under the plan, WNISR said.
The plan brings forward the completion of 10 semiconductor factories to 2040 from the mid-2040s and adds four more in Gwangju, which would need 6.3 GW.
AI data centres would need 18.4 GW, including 8.4 GW by 2029 and a further 10 GW by 2035.
“Combined, this brings the total power requirements, in addition to previously planned expansions, to 27.7GW by 2040,” WNISR said.
The plan states that "all available power generation sources will be utilised", whilst it aims to reach 100 GW of renewables by 2030 and says nuclear power and small modular reactors (SMRs) "will be actively utilised".
WNISR said SMRs will not be available by 2030.
The existing 11th Basic Plan for Long-Term Electricity Supply and Demand includes two 1.4 GW large plants due in 2037 and 2038 and four 175-megawatt (MW) SMR modules due in 2034 and 2035.
The government will decide whether to add more nuclear plants, including SMRs, in its 12th power plan, due by the end of 2026, Climate, Energy and Environment Minister Kim Seong-hwan said in July.
The Korean Nuclear Society said in February 2026 that at least 20 large plants and 12 SMRs would be needed by 2050.
President Lee Jae-myung said in September 2025 that building more nuclear plants was "not a realistic option", but said in January 2026 that overturning policies "simply because the administration has changed is not beneficial".
SK hynix used 13.7 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2025, more than the 10.35TWh used by Daejeon, a city of over 1.4 million people.

articles.title: The vanishing word in Trump’s North Korea diplomacy - Lowy Institute
articles.summary: The vanishing word in Trump’s North Korea diplomacy  Lowy Institute
articles.full_text:
A 2017 protest in Berlin against US–North Korea nuclear escalation (Omer Messinger/Getty Images)
The vanishing word in Trump’s North Korea diplomacy
Denuclearisation is off the table, and the next US deal with Pyongyang will test the limits of extended deterrence.
US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping discussed North Korea in their recent meeting, but the absence of a particular word was striking.
“Denuclearisation” was nowhere to be heard.
Neither the US fact sheet (Opens in new window) released following the talks nor Chinese media (Opens in new window) reports (Opens in new window) of the summit mentioned denuclearisation, which for years had been the main focus of diplomacy around the Korean Peninsula. The omission nudges Trump closer to China’s position (Opens in new window) on North Korea’s nuclear program, and appears part of his push (Opens in new window) for a further summit with North Korean Chairman Kim Jong-un, with China positioning itself (Opens in new window) as the broker.
The missing word also reflects the reality of the moment. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung supports (Opens in new window) a freeze, not elimination of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program. North Korea has pledged (Opens in new window) not to give up its nuclear weapons. An arms control (Opens in new window) arrangement is likely to be the main agenda of a fourth Trump–Kim summit, if it materialises.
Past (Opens in new window) arms control attempts involved proposals that the United States would give North Korea a security guarantee and sanctions relief in exchange for a reduction – and an eventual total elimination – of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal. But the next round of arms control talks will revolve around how the United States lives with a nuclear-armed North Korea in perpetuity, while keeping the US–South Korea alliance intact and dissuading Seoul from going nuclear.
An arms control deal with North Korea may counterintuitively create a proliferation problem with South Korea.
How those objectives can be achieved starts with understanding how negotiations have gone before and where both sides may get stuck.
Washington reserves the option of launching a first (Opens in new window) strike against an enemy’s nuclear weapons before it can use them. Such a policy allows (Opens in new window) Washington to assure South Korea of the credibility of its extended deterrence.
But in 1991, the United States decided to withdraw (Opens in new window) tactical nuclear weapons from South Korea as an exchange for North Korea allowing inspections of its nuclear facilities. North Korea criticised (Opens in new window) the US gesture as insufficient to guarantee North Korea’s survival, believing Washington could still use its long-range weapons based outside of the Korean Peninsula to attack it. The 1994 Agreed Framework thus included (Opens in new window) a US assurance not to use force or threat of force including nuclear weapons against North Korea. The assurance against a first strike is important because an arms control deal would freeze North Korea’s nuclear development, thus capping the number of targets and revealing their locations to the United States.
After the Agreed Framework collapsed in 2003, North Korea demanded (Opens in new window) a formal non-aggression treaty with the United States during the Six-Party Talks (2003–09), which then US President George W. Bush countered (Opens in new window) with a five-party security guarantee of the United States, China, Russia, Japan, and South Korea. Pyongyang rejected (Opens in new window) the counterproposal because it viewed the security guarantee as a bilateral issue with Washington and only a treaty would commit future US administrations to non-aggression.
The United States did not want a non-aggression treaty with North Korea because it wished (Opens in new window) to avoid involving the Senate into the formal process of a treaty. It saw a legally non-binding (Opens in new window) agreement without Senate ratification as sufficient. Washington offered a non-aggression agreement in 2013, but Pyongyang rejected (Opens in new window) it. Neither the 2012 (Opens in new window) Leap Day deal nor the 2018 (Opens in new window) Trump–Kim joint statement includes an explicit legally binding US security guarantee. Of course, neither side signed an arms control deal.
A binding non-aggression treaty with the United States would offer North Korea a security guarantee that both alliance treaties with Russia and China cannot. North Korea’s alliance treaties with Russia and China are binding (Opens in new window) in case of a US first strike, but how these partners respond to such a strike remains uncertain. If the first strike only targets nuclear sites with minimal collateral damage and doesn’t pose a threat to the Kim regime, Moscow and Beijing may not retaliate in full force to avoid fighting a nuclear war with Washington. North Korea would have to restart its nuclear program should a US first strike succeed. A binding non-aggression treaty means North Korea will not have to worry about such a strike after agreeing to an arms control deal.
Washington is stuck in a dilemma. Not signing a non-aggression treaty with North Korea diminishes the prospect of an arms control deal and leaving its nuclear program growing unrestrained. Signing one, however, might mean South Korea will doubt the credibility of extended deterrence. Seoul may pursue an independent nuclear program to address decoupling (Opens in new window).
A successful arms control deal means the United States will have to balance between assuring North Korea that it will not launch a first strike and assuring South Korea that it will trade Seattle for Seoul. Neither option is easy to achieve. An arms control with North Korea may counterintuitively create a proliferation problem with South Korea.

articles.title: Korean Chip Patent Suits in U.S. Hit Record High This Year - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korean Chip Patent Suits in U.S. Hit Record High This Year  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Patent lawsuits in the United States involving South Korean companies in the semiconductor sector have hit a record high this year. As chips emerge as a core industrial asset for governments and Korean chipmakers post their best-ever earnings, disputes over patent infringement are multiplying.
Data from the Korea Intellectual Property Protection Agency, obtained by The Seoul Economic Daily, showed 18 semiconductor patent lawsuits involving Korean companies in the U.S. through the end of July. The seven-month tally alone exceeds the highest annual figure since the agency began compiling the statistics in 2012. Annual totals were 10 cases in 2024 and eight last year. This is the first time a breakdown of semiconductor-only cases has been disclosed from the broader count of U.S. patent suits involving Korean companies.
Of this year's disputes, Korean companies were defendants in nine cases, also a record. There were six such cases in each of 2024 and last year. Suits filed by Korean companies in the U.S. also reached nine, matching the annual record set in 2022. With months left in the year, both filings and defenses are likely to exceed 10 each, pushing the total above 20.
SK hynix (000660) was sued for patent infringement in the U.S. in May. The plaintiff alleged that SK hynix used its patented technologies, including a three-dimensional vertical stacking structure and transistor layout, without authorization in making high-bandwidth memory. Notably, the plaintiff is not a rival chipmaker but a non-practicing entity, Monolithic 3D. SK hynix had also been sued by the same firm in February.
The SK hynix case illustrates the pattern of U.S. semiconductor patent litigation that Korean companies face. Foreign non-practicing entities allege infringement by large Korean chipmakers and ask U.S. federal district courts to settle the claims. Suits targeting Korean companies have climbed to a record this year, particularly as the chip market booms.
According to the agency, non-practicing entities were the plaintiffs in 17 of the 24 U.S. semiconductor patent suits filed against Korean companies over the five years through the end of July, or 70.8%. Of this year's nine cases, seven, or 77.8%, were brought by such entities. Non-practicing entities own no production facilities; they buy patents and generate revenue by enforcing them, claiming other companies used their patents without permission and extracting settlements, damages or royalties.
Behind the rise in these disputes is the intent of non-practicing entities to extract money from Korean companies. Their targets are typically large corporations with the financial capacity to pay settlements or damages. As the chip boom put Samsung Electronics (005930) and SK hynix on track for record operating profit, the entities naturally turned their attention to the two companies. Kim Yong-sun, commissioner of the Korea Intellectual Property Administration, said in a recent interview with this newspaper that "the larger semiconductors loom in Korean industry, the more noticeable it becomes that foreign NPEs are generating patent disputes in the chip sector."
U.S. policy has also fueled the increase. Since President Donald Trump took office, the administration has strengthened its policy stance on protecting U.S. companies' patent rights. One example is the more frequent rejection by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office of inter partes review petitions, a key defense for companies being sued. Backed by that stance, U.S. non-practicing entities have become more active than before.
Korean companies, by contrast, have few tools in court against such entities. Non-practicing entities only enforce patents; they do not make or sell products using the technology. In a dispute between manufacturers, a company can counter-sue using its own patents, but against a non-practicing entity, even a large company's patent portfolio offers no means of attack. As a result, defendants often settle regardless of whether infringement actually occurred, out of concern over litigation costs and reputational damage, industry officials said.
Core memory chip technologies have recently become targets as well. Following SK hynix, Samsung Electronics was sued in June over high-bandwidth memory by Mare Infinitus, another non-practicing entity. The patents at issue in both cases cover technologies considered central to high-bandwidth memory, including the three-dimensional vertical stacking structure and through-silicon via technology. These are used not only in high-bandwidth memory but also in NAND flash. Because the suits target core memory technologies, the industry is watching closely for whether the disputes spread to other products.
Midsize companies have also been drawn in. Everlight Electronics, a Taiwanese light-emitting diode maker, filed a patent suit against Seoul Semiconductor (046890) in the U.S. in February. It is the first time Seoul Semiconductor has been sued over semiconductor patents. Everlight based its claim not on technology it developed itself but on patents it had purchased from other companies. The case has drawn industry attention as a contest between a Taiwanese and a Korean company in a U.S. court.
Korean companies are not only on the receiving end. Of the nine U.S. semiconductor patent suits filed by Korean companies this year, a substantial share came from Korean non-practicing entities. As intellectual property rights grow in importance, such a business is taking shape in Korea as well. Domestic entities increasingly buy patents from small companies or research institutes and then enforce them against foreign firms. Patent disputes once consisted mainly of foreign entities suing Korean companies, but a new pattern has emerged in which Korean entities sue foreign ones.
The most worrying scenario as these disputes intensify is a restriction on chip exports to the U.S. Some cases proceed through the U.S. International Trade Commission, which can issue exclusion orders barring imports of products found to infringe patents. Such products would then face limits on import and distribution in the U.S. A worst case in which an ITC ruling halts chip exports to the country cannot be ruled out.
Experts say perceptions of U.S. semiconductor patent litigation need to change. Noh Jae-il, head of the Korea Intellectual Property Management Association, said: "An ITC exclusion order could shake our industry's entire chip supply chain. It is time to treat semiconductor patent disputes as a trade issue for a strategic industry."
Others point to shortcomings in Korea's own framework. Sung Yun-mo, chair of the steering committee of the Intellectual Property Strategy Forum and a former minister of trade, industry and energy, said: "In the U.S., federal policy supporting legitimate patent enforcement and state policy restraining indiscriminate patent suits are developing together. Korea, by contrast, has not sufficiently discussed support for helping key industries avoid patent infringement, or a framework for monetizing patent rights at home and abroad." He added that "the government and the private sector need to work together on new rules."

USD/JPY holds firm on Tuesday as the Japanese Yen (JPY) trades on the defensive across the board. However, a softer US Dollar (USD), weighed down by a pullback in US Treasury yields, and intervention concerns around the 160 level limit the upside, keeping the pair range-bound. At the time of writing, USD/JPY trades around 158, up 0.10% on the day.
The Japanese Yen struggles to gain traction as Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterates the case for further tightening while leaving the timing and pace of future rate hikes dependent on economic developments.
Speaking on Tuesday, Ueda said, “We're to keep raising rates in response to the economy and inflation.” However, he added that the “pace and timing of future policy adjustment will be decided based on the likelihood of our baseline projections materialising, as well as risks.”
Ueda also flagged the possibility of underlying inflation exceeding the BoJ’s 2% target, citing pressures associated with the Middle East conflict, AI-related demand and persistent Yen weakness. His remarks keep further rate increases on the table but offer limited guidance on whether the central bank will act at its October 29-30 meeting.
Analysts also link the Yen’s softer tone to a Bloomberg report published on Monday that Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) did not discuss portfolio allocation at its September meeting. The report dampened hopes that the fund would bring money back to Japan to invest in domestic assets.
On the US side, Treasury yields retreat as the recent bond selloff pauses. The benchmark 10-year yield falls to around 5.27% after reaching 5.349% on Monday, its highest level since 2002. The decline takes some support away from the Greenback. The US Dollar Index (DXY), which tracks the Greenback’s value against a basket of six major currencies, retreats toward 101.80 after reaching a fresh year-to-date high of 102.53 the previous day.
Even so, inflation and fiscal concerns keep US yields elevated, preserving a wide gap with Japanese yields and maintaining the appeal of US Dollar-denominated assets.
On the monetary policy front, the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) broader outlook remains hawkish as policymakers work to bring inflation back toward the 2% target. However, softer-than-expected Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) and Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation data released last week have reduced pressure on the Fed to raise rates at its October 27-28 meeting. articles.title: South Korean diplomacy: the wheels are coming off - The Korea Times
articles.summary: South Korean diplomacy: the wheels are coming off  The Korea Times

Since President Lee Jae Myung entered office in June 2025, I have mostly complimented his administration’s foreign policy. Alas, the wheels are coming off. Before we get to the current situation — with Seoul flailing on U.S., Ukraine and North Korea issues — let’s review the trajectory until now.
When Lee took office, he faced a difficult diplomatic environment. Above all, Seoul was under competing pressures from Washington and Beijing. The U.S. under President Donald Trump was increasingly demanding of allies — including Seoul — in the realms of security and economics. Meanwhile China remained a tricky economic partner for South Korean industry and a regional security actor with inscrutable goals on North Korea. Upgrading other bilateral relations was important, both per se and as means for creating more autonomy vis-à-vis the U.S. and China. To this end, Seoul continued to enhance strategic partnerships — e.g., with Japan, Europe, Australia, Singapore and Canada — while emphasizing relations with Global South states with significant commercial or resource profiles.
An important multilateral diplomatic calendar also loomed — a mid-June G7 summit, late-June NATO summit, September U.N. General Assembly, October APEC summit hosted in Gyeongju and December G20 meeting.
The Lee administration largely acquitted itself well, notably on key bilateral issues and the APEC summit. South Korea stood firm as a U.S. ally while patiently resisting excessive U.S. trade and investment demands. Seoul’s trade relations with Beijing stayed on track, and China even removed controversial facilities from the China-South Korea Provisional Maritime Zone. Entente with Japan continued apace, to the surprise of many, given the contentious history of Seoul-Tokyo relations under prior progressive presidents. Outreach to other strategic partners and the Global South established a conveyor belt of memoranda of understanding on economic relations, supply chains, critical resources and other cooperation areas that may mitigate some of the risks Seoul experiences in being caught between Washington and Beijing.
APEC in Gyeongju was successful, both multilaterally and in terms of bilateral meetings surrounding it. The most important was a Trump-Lee summit that — in principle — established a U.S-South Korea trade and investment agreement and opened the door to a South Korean nuclear-powered submarine deal that includes potential rights for Seoul to develop uranium enrichment and spent nuclear fuel reprocessing capabilities.
However, the end of 2025 marked the high point of Lee’s diplomacy, and it has been mostly a downhill slide ever since. In January 2026, the Trump administration began voicing displeasure at Seoul’s implementation of the trade and investment deal. In January and February, U.S.-South Korea discord over the treatment of online delivery platform Coupang began disrupting progress in other areas, including security and defense. Also in February a kerfuffle emerged over the scheduling of U.S.-South Korea-Japan trilateral air exercises. Spring and summer were marked by the effect of the U.S. war against Iran, which both affected South Korea’s economy and occasioned Trump to coerce Lee into joining the war. This reached a climax with an angry social media post in which Trump insulted Lee and South Korea, praised North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, curtailed U.S.-South Korea military exercises and again pressured Seoul to enter the Iran conflict. All this was accompanied by growing influence of the “autonomy” faction of South Korea’s progressive foreign policy apparatus, which began to crank up obsequious, ineffective outreach to Pyongyang. They also added a wrinkle by attempting — for reasons involving commercial relations, natural resources, arctic shipping and North Korea — to get the Lee administration to accommodate Putin’s Russia, thus irritating European and Canadian partners.
Currently the diplomatic wheels are off the rails. Washington and Seoul publicly dispute the status of South Korean investment into an Alaska LNG project — a deliverable for the U.S.-South Korea trade and investment deal. Consequently Trump is threatening to punish Seoul financially. The submarine deal may also be endangered. The transfer to South Korea of North Korean POWs held by Ukraine has devolved into a rhetorical fight between Seoul and Kyiv over whether the POWs’ repatriation should have been announced. Regardless of which side is right, Seoul would have been better served to keep the argument quiet. A North Korean land mine that exploded in the DMZ, injuring South Korean soldiers, has backfooted Lee’s administration. In demanding a North Korean apology while also downplaying the incident as an “unfortunate accident,” Seoul is incoherently both making it a big deal and providing Pyongyang with cover. Unsurprisingly, the media report that the National Security Council’s “autonomy” and “alliance” factions are deeply divided over the response.
How did Lee’s diplomacy go from hero to zero? Beyond intra-government ideological rifts, domestic politics play a role. Lee’s weakened poll numbers are causing ruling party frustration, with the “autonomy” faction using increased influence to underline South Korean sovereignty as an appeal to base supporters of the Democratic Party of Korea.
This probably won’t work domestically. It’s definitely failing diplomatically. The next risk is that the administration doubles down and gins ups problems with Japan. In that case, the train will likely be not only off the rails, but over the cliff.
Mason Richey is a professor of international politics at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies and president of the Korea International Studies Association.

Market reaction
At the time of writing, the USD/JPY pair is up 0.18% on the day at 158.20.
Ueda keeps BoJ on gradual tightening path as Yen focus stays on inflation
FXS Speechtracker scores the speech at 7.2, exactly in line with Ueda’s historic average, signaling a consistent policy tone rather than a surprise shift. The emphasis on the economy “recovering moderately,” favorable business sentiment, and accommodative financial conditions, even after the September rate hike, points to a mildly hawkish bias, as BoJ remains committed to further gradual rate increases while avoiding aggressive tightening.
By stressing that underlying inflation is approaching 2% and that economy and prices are moving in line with baseline forecasts, Ueda reinforces confidence that BoJ is on track toward the inflation target, which supports a constructive backdrop for the Yen. The pledge to “continue to raise policy rate” in accordance with economic, price, and financial developments, and the importance of anchoring inflation around 2%, underpins expectations of a slow but ongoing normalization, likely offering medium-term support to the Yen while limiting immediate volatility.
Japanese Yen FAQs
The Japanese Yen (JPY) is one of the world’s most traded currencies. Its value is broadly determined by the performance of the Japanese economy, but more specifically by the Bank of Japan’s policy, the differential between Japanese and US bond yields, or risk sentiment among traders, among other factors.
One of the Bank of Japan’s mandates is currency control, so its moves are key for the Yen. The BoJ has directly intervened in currency markets sometimes, generally to lower the value of the Yen, although it refrains from doing it often due to political concerns of its main trading partners. The BoJ ultra-loose monetary policy between 2013 and 2024 caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks. More recently, the gradually unwinding of this ultra-loose policy has given some support to the Yen.
Over the last decade, the BoJ’s stance of sticking to ultra-loose monetary policy has led to a widening policy divergence with other central banks, particularly with the US Federal Reserve. This supported a widening of the differential between the 10-year US and Japanese bonds, which favored the US Dollar against the Japanese Yen. The BoJ decision in 2024 to gradually abandon the ultra-loose policy, coupled with interest-rate cuts in other major central banks, is narrowing this differential.
The Japanese Yen is often seen as a safe-haven investment. This means that in times of market stress, investors are more likely to put their money in the Japanese currency due to its supposed reliability and stability. Turbulent times are likely to strengthen the Yen’s value against other currencies seen as more risky to invest in.

articles.title: AI boom spreads beyond Korean chipmakers to components and cooling - Aju Press
articles.summary: AI boom spreads beyond Korean chipmakers to components and cooling  Aju Press
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, October 06 (AJP) -The AI boom is spilling beyond South Korea’s chipmakers, driving orders and investment in the components that stabilize power, connect processors and keep data centers from overheating.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics on Tuesday disclosed a $210.24 million AI-server capacitor contract, bringing its announced long-term supply agreements this year to about 3.9 trillion won. LG Electronics on the same day announced a deal to supply cooling systems for 5 gigawatts of AI data center capacity in North America.
The deals show how growing computing requirements are expanding demand across the infrastructure surrounding AI chips. More powerful processors need a stable electricity supply, increasingly sophisticated connections and cooling systems capable of removing concentrated heat.
Investors turned to the stocks while dumping bigger chipmakers. At 3:00 p.m. Seoul time, Samsung Electro-Mechanics was up 5.19 percent at 1,663,000 won, while LG Electronics gained 7.18 percent to 231,500 won, according to Korea Investment & Securities market data. Shares of SK hynix fell 3.5 percent and Samsung Electronics 1.5 percent.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ latest contract covers multilayer ceramic capacitors, or MLCCs, supplied to an unidentified global company throughout 2027.
The filing valued the agreement at 285.6 billion won, equivalent to 2.5 percent of the company’s 2025 consolidated revenue. It is the sixth long-term supply agreement the company has disclosed this year, following another contract worth about 285 billion won on Sept. 29.
MLCCs store and release electrical energy to stabilize power supplied to chips and suppress electrical noise. AI servers require high-capacity components that can withstand demanding temperatures, voltages and continuous operation.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics says AI servers can contain more than 10 times as many MLCCs as conventional servers. It estimates its share of the AI-server MLCC market at more than 40 percent.
The company cites a Goldman Sachs forecast that the market will grow from $1.4 billion in 2025 to $5.8 billion in 2030, an annual compound growth rate of about 33 percent.
“Customer requirements for high-performance MLCCs continue to rise alongside the growth of the AI market,” a Samsung Electro-Mechanics official said. “We will expand the share of AI-use MLCC products based on our technology and stable supply capabilities.”
The company is also committing 6.78 trillion won to expand production of advanced semiconductor packaging substrates in South Korea and Vietnam.
These substrates, known as flip-chip ball grid arrays, connect processors to circuit boards and carry electrical signals and power. As AI chips become more complex, the substrates must accommodate larger dimensions, more layers and denser connections.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics will invest 4.27 trillion won at its Sejong operation, with mass production scheduled to begin in September 2028. Another 2.51 trillion won will go toward equipment for its Vietnamese expansion, where completion and operation are targeted for June 2030.
The company said customer funding support and medium- to long-term volume commitments would help reduce the financial and utilization risks of the expansion.
Its U.S. unit signed a long-term agreement with AIR Control Concepts to supply high-efficiency chillers and other cooling systems in phases for 5 gigawatts of North American AI data center capacity. Financial terms and a detailed delivery schedule were not disclosed.
The agreement follows LG’s Oct. 1 announcement of a 150 billion won investment in a new U.S. chiller factory and expanded production lines in South Korea.
The factory in Windsor, Virginia, is scheduled to begin production in the first half of 2027. It will manufacture air-cooled chillers for AI data centers, giving LG a local production base to serve the North American market.
LG is also adding air-cooled chiller production lines and upgrading equipment at its Pyeongtaek and Changwon plants, with the domestic expansion proceeding in stages through the end of 2026.
Chillers remove heat from water circulated through cooling systems. As AI processors become more powerful and densely packed, that heat-management infrastructure is essential to sustaining performance and preventing overheating.
LG is broadening its offering into what it calls “chip-to-chiller” cooling: cold plates that absorb heat directly from processors, coolant distribution units that circulate and manage cooling fluid, and chillers that remove the collected heat.
The company and AIR are discussing extending their partnership to coolant distribution units, linking the latest supply agreement to LG’s broader liquid-cooling business.
LG said orders for its AI data center cooling solutions exceeded 600 billion won in the first half of 2026 and are expected to reach several trillion won by year-end.
The company is also pursuing projects beyond North America. In Indonesia, it is supplying solutions for a large AI data center being developed by Sinar Mas Group in Jakarta, combining its cooling technology with LG Energy Solution’s batteries and LG CNS’s data center design, construction and operating capabilities.
“We will continue to strengthen our ability to supply cooling solutions reliably as core infrastructure for AI data centers, and actively respond to rapidly growing market demand,” said Lee Jae-sung, president of LG’s Eco Solution business.

articles.title: South Korea's Top 1% Investors Pile Into Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Exit Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix - BigGo Finance

South Korea's top 1% highest-return investors over the past month continued their concentrated buying of electrical and electronic component stocks on the 6th, with Samsung Electro-Mechanics emerging as their most aggressive purchase. In contrast, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both facing the imminent conclusion of their large-scale share buyback programs, remained among the top net sells, showing a starkly divergent trend.
According to Mirae Asset Securities' tally of trading activity among its top 1% highest-return customers, Samsung Electro-Mechanics was the No. 1 net buy as of 2:30 p.m. The stock traded at 1.667 million won (approximately $1,200), up 5.44% from the previous session. It had already claimed the top net buy position in the 9:30 a.m. tally and maintained that ranking throughout the session.
The buying momentum in Samsung Electro-Mechanics was driven by a string of supply agreements with major global corporations. The company disclosed on the same day that it had signed a 285.6 billion won (approximately $213.3 million) supply contract with a global enterprise for AI server multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs). This marks the sixth long-term supply agreement this year, with cumulative contract value estimated at approximately 4 trillion won (approximately $3.0 billion).
On the 29th of last month, the company also signed a 290 billion won (approximately $216.5 million) supply agreement with a global enterprise for AI server MLCCs and inductors. Brokerages have been issuing a steady stream of forecasts that Samsung Electro-Mechanics' earnings growth will accelerate. Korea Investment & Securities recently raised its target price on Samsung Electro-Mechanics to 2.4 million won (approximately $1,800). Hwang Jun-tae, an analyst at Korea Investment & Securities, wrote in a report: "We believe MLCCs, Samsung Electro-Mechanics' flagship product, have entered the early stages of a price upcycle. For silicon capacitors, the company signed a 1.557 trillion won (approximately $1.2 billion) supply agreement with a global enterprise, and we estimate revenue of 500 billion won in 2025 and 1 trillion won (approximately $746.7 million) by 2028."
KB Securities also projected that Samsung Electro-Mechanics' third-quarter operating profit would reach an all-time high. With the KOSPI trading slightly lower near the 7,000-point level, Samsung Electro-Mechanics posted the highest share price gain among the top 10 market-cap stocks, further fueling investor sentiment.
Buying Spreads to LG Electronics and LG Innotek
While buying was concentrated in semiconductor substrate and component stocks in the morning, LG Electronics and LG Innotek rose to the No. 2 and No. 3 net buy positions in the afternoon, broadening the buying scope across the electrical and electronics sector.
LG Electronics, the No. 2 net buy, traded at 232,000 won (approximately $170), up 7.41%. News that LG Electronics had signed a long-term contract to supply a total of 5 gigawatts (GW) of cooling solutions to North American AI data centers (AIDCs) served as the direct catalyst for the share price surge. As of the first half of this year, LG Electronics' AI data center cooling solution orders exceeded 600 billion won (approximately $448.0 million), and the company expects the figure to reach the multi-trillion won range by year-end.
Meritz Securities also raised its target price on LG Electronics from 220,000 won (approximately $160) to 250,000 won (approximately $190), citing the growth potential of its AI data center cooling and robotics businesses.
LG Innotek surged 11.5% to 640,000 won (approximately $480), ranking as the No. 3 net buy. Kiwoom Securities noted that while LG Innotek's third-quarter results are expected to fall short of market expectations, the shortfall is temporary due to currency effects, and maintained its buy rating with a target price of 1.1 million won (approximately $820).
In early morning trading, semiconductor substrate and component stocks such as TLb, Simmtech, and Hana Micron also featured prominently among the top net buys. TLb rose 4.75% to 50,750 won (approximately $38) as the No. 2 net buy, while Simmtech gained 6.1% to 177,400 won (approximately $130) at No. 3. Hana Micron climbed 3.69% to 53,400 won (approximately $40), ranking fourth.
Large-Cap Semiconductor Stocks See Outflows Ahead of Buyback Completion
The top net sells among the highest-return investors were Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Doosan. As of 11 a.m., Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were down 0.36% and 2.39%, respectively, from the previous session.
The selling pressure on both stocks is attributed to concerns over a supply-demand vacuum as their large-scale share buyback programs near completion. Since mid-August, when both companies announced their massive buybacks, other corporate entities have been purchasing an average of 1 trillion won (approximately $746.7 million) worth of shares per day, providing support to the market. However, with the buyback completion dates approaching in mid-to-late October, investor exits are becoming a reality.
At the same time, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix ranked No. 1 and No. 4, respectively, among foreign investors' net sells, indicating that not only the top 1% investors but also foreign investors are taking a net selling stance.
On the previous trading day, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Jeju Semiconductor, Industrial Bank of Korea, and Samsung Electronics preferred shares topped the net buy list, while Samsung Electronics, Doosan, TES, SK Hynix, and TMC were among the top net sells. The top investors' buying of Samsung Electro-Mechanics has continued since the prior session, suggesting that their preference for AI-related component stocks is not a short-term phenomenon but an established trend.
