articles.title: Korea's Household Debt Ratio Falls to 10-Year Low on Faster GDP Growth - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korea's Household Debt Ratio Falls to 10-Year Low on Faster GDP Growth  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
South Korea's household debt as a share of nominal gross domestic product fell to its lowest level in 10 years at the end of the second quarter. Household debt continued to rise, but nominal GDP grew faster, according to the data.
The ratio of household debt to GDP stood at 81.1% at the end of the second quarter, the Bank of Korea said on the 7th in its flow of funds statistics for the second quarter of 2026. That was down 4.2 percentage points from 85.3% in the previous quarter and the lowest since the second quarter of 2016, when the ratio was 80.2%.
The government has set a target of lowering the ratio to around 80% by 2030, meaning the ratio is now approaching that 2030 target well ahead of schedule.
Net lending by households and nonprofit organizations — funds invested minus funds raised — totaled 60.7 trillion won in the second quarter, down 18.5 trillion won from 79.2 trillion won in the previous quarter. The central bank attributed the decline to lower income and a rise in net home purchases, which left households with less surplus cash.
Excluding funds raised, households invested 88.5 trillion won in the second quarter, down 7.8 trillion won from 96.3 trillion won in the prior quarter. Investment in equities and investment funds rose sharply to 101.6 trillion won from 61.4 trillion won, but 23.3 trillion won flowed out of deposits at financial institutions, reducing the overall total.
Net lending by nonfinancial corporations surged, driven by a jump in net profit led by chipmakers. The figure more than tripled to 67.1 trillion won in the second quarter from 20.8 trillion won in the first quarter, the highest since the data series began in 2009.
Funds invested by nonfinancial corporations climbed to 267.1 trillion won from 137 trillion won, while funds raised rose to 200 trillion won from 116.2 trillion won. The much larger increase in funds invested drove the sharp rise in net lending.
The general government swung to net lending of 11.1 trillion won. The central bank said the shift from net borrowing came as government revenue grew faster than spending.

articles.title: Why Marvell Stock Is Surging: Google AI Chip Ties and the $20B Revenue Target - MEXC
articles.summary: Why Marvell Stock Is Surging: Google AI Chip Ties and the $20B Revenue Target  MEXC
articles.full_text:
Overview
 
Marvell Technology raised its fiscal 2028 revenue target to roughly $20 billion at its October 6 investor day, and the stock closed at $287.01, up 5.81%, after gaining close to 10% intraday, leaving the company valued at about $251.7 billion according to StockAnalysis's MRVL data page. Broadcom rose about 4% in sympathy the same day.
 
The single headline number is not what reset expectations. Management also lifted its fiscal 2029 custom-chip revenue goal from $10 billion to more than $12 billion and framed a fiscal 2031 revenue range of $70 billion to $90 billion. Against a prior analyst estimate of roughly $46.85 billion for fiscal 2031, that target says management believes hyperscaler demand for in-house AI silicon is materially larger than sell-side models assume. Google sits at the center of that thesis, and the agreement the two companies signed in late July already ties order volume to equity through a warrant.
 
 
Key Takeaways
 
The raise is far wider than a normal beat. Reuters reported that the $20 billion fiscal 2028 target exceeds a Wall Street consensus of $18.2 billion, while the fiscal 2031 midpoint of $80 billion is roughly 1.7 times the analyst estimate.
 
Custom silicon targets moved up by a fifth. Per Investing.com's account of the investor day, the fiscal 2029 custom-chip goal rose from $10 billion to above $12 billion, with a fiscal 2031 earnings target of $30 or more per share.
 
Interconnect, not custom compute, is the largest bucket. Within the $80 billion midpoint for fiscal 2031, interconnect accounts for roughly $37.5 billion against about $30 billion for custom compute and $10 billion for switching and storage, so the AI story here is as much about connectivity as about ASICs.
 
The $120 billion figure has a precise origin. Marvell's 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission sets warrant vesting at one tranche per $500 million of custom product revenue across 240 tranches, which is exactly the cumulative revenue behind the widely quoted headline.
 
The gap to Broadcom remains wide. Broadcom's third-quarter results filed with regulators show $16.7 billion of AI semiconductor revenue in a single quarter, more than Marvell's full-year custom-chip target for fiscal 2029.
 
Customer concentration is the other side of the thesis. Marvell's fiscal 2026 annual report discloses one direct customer at 14% of net revenue and one distributor at 37%, together more than half the business.
 
The Numbers That Actually Moved Expectations
 
From Fiscal 2028 to Fiscal 2031
 
The event took place in New York, as set out in the August announcement. The target structure runs on several levels: roughly $20 billion of revenue in fiscal 2028, of which about $18 billion is data center; more than $12 billion of custom-chip revenue in fiscal 2029; and $70 billion to $90 billion of revenue in fiscal 2031 with earnings of $30 or more per share. Chief Executive Matt Murphy also put the addressable market at about $400 billion by 2030.
 
Those figures need the current base for context. Marvell's second-quarter filing for the period ended August 1, 2026 shows record revenue of $2.739 billion, up 37% year over year, with data center at $2.172 billion, or 79% of the total, up 46%, and third-quarter guidance of $3.15 billion plus or minus 5%. Annualizing the current run rate puts the business near $12 billion, so reaching $20 billion by fiscal 2028 implies something close to a doubling over two years, and the fiscal 2031 midpoint implies quadrupling again from there.
 
Targets are not results, but they move the valuation anchor. The market had been pricing Marvell against roughly $46.85 billion of fiscal 2031 revenue and about $19 of earnings per share. Management substituted $80 billion and $30. The move in the share price is the first instalment of the market's discount applied to that new anchor.
 
 
The session was not one-directional. Investing.com records the stock down 3% as the meeting opened, up as much as 10% at the peak and closing 5.90% higher. StockAnalysis puts the close at $287.01, up 5.81%, against a 52-week range of $70.69 to $329.88, a spread that itself shows how violently this company has been repriced over the past year.
 
The spillover matters more than the move. Reuters noted Broadcom rose about 4% the same day. The two do not compete for the same sockets, but they share one assumption: hyperscalers will keep shifting AI workloads toward custom silicon rather than general-purpose GPUs. Marvell quantified that assumption over five years, and the market applied it to Broadcom by extension.
 
Why Custom Silicon Became the Main Story
 
How ASICs and General-Purpose GPUs Divide the Work
 
Custom silicon in this context means an application-specific integrated circuit, co-developed by a chip supplier and a cloud provider for one customer's workloads. It trades flexibility for performance per watt and lower unit cost on the target task. Google's tensor processing units are the most mature example. According to Google Cloud's official release notes, TPU7x, the first member of the seventh-generation Ironwood family, entered preview on November 24, 2025 and reached general availability on March 31, 2026, supporting training and inference for large language models, mixture-of-experts models and diffusion models.
 
The distinction worth preserving is division of labor rather than substitution. A general-purpose GPU earns its premium through adaptability, since architectures, frameworks and kernels change every few months, while an ASIC takes one to two years from specification to volume. For training runs against moving targets, the GPU remains the lower-risk choice. For inference at stable architectures running the same operation endlessly, the cost advantage of custom silicon fully lands. That is why Google expands its own accelerators while continuing to buy from Nvidia.
 
Inference Economics Did the Repricing
 
The variable behind this wave is the sheer scale of inference. Nvidia reported revenue of $96.2 billion for the quarter ended July 26, 2026, including $89.0 billion from data center, up 117% year over year, in its second-quarter results, where Chief Executive Jensen Huang described the moment as one where compute is revenue and demand is accelerating. At that volume of token generation, a single percentage point of unit cost compounds into billions of dollars, and the payback on a dedicated design becomes straightforward.
 
Capital budgets corroborate it. On Alphabet's second-quarter call, Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi raised full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $195 billion to $205 billion from $180 billion to $190 billion, with roughly 60% directed at servers and 40% at data centers and networking equipment, per the transcript published by Investing.com. Management also noted that external TPU system sales already sit in the cloud backlog with most revenue expected in 2027. For suppliers, that is both the source of order visibility and the reason targets are set on fiscal 2028 rather than today.
 
What the Google Agreement Actually Binds
 
A Warrant That Converts Revenue Into Equity
 
The 8-K rewards a close read. Marvell and Google entered a commercial partnership on July 29, 2026 covering development of custom semiconductor products including AI inference accelerators, storage controllers and network interface controllers. As part of it, Marvell issued Google a warrant over 58,970,907 common shares at an exercise price of $206.58, expiring August 18, 2033.
 
Vesting splits in two. A time-based portion of 1,360,867 shares vests quarterly across the first year. The remainder vests against revenue, divided into 240 equal tranches, with one tranche vesting per $500 million of custom product revenue from the third quarter of fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2033.
 
Where the $120 Billion Comes From
 
Run the vesting schedule through simple arithmetic and the headline resolves itself. Two hundred and forty tranches at a $500 million revenue threshold each equals $120 billion, matching Reuters' description of a partnership that could generate up to roughly $120 billion in sales through fiscal 2033 if performance milestones are achieved. The number describes the cumulative revenue required for full vesting. It is a ceiling assumption, not a signed purchase commitment.
 
The structure cuts both ways for shareholders. It aligns the customer with the supplier's equity and lowers the odds of the socket being handed to a rival. It also means that the more revenue arrives, the more dilution arrives with it. At the October 6 close of $287.01 against the $206.58 strike, each tranche of roughly 240,000 shares carries about $19 million of intrinsic value, close to 4% of the $500 million of revenue that triggers it. That cost never shows up in gross margin, but it lives permanently in the denominator of earnings per share.
 
 
The Distance to Broadcom
 
Broadcom still owns this category by a wide margin. Its third quarter ended August 2, 2026 delivered revenue of $29.6 billion, up 86%, including $16.7 billion of AI semiconductor revenue, up 221% year over year and 54% sequentially, with fourth-quarter guidance of $34.8 billion in total revenue and $21.7 billion from AI semiconductors. Chief Executive Hock Tan said demand for custom AI accelerators and networking remains very strong.
 
Placed side by side, the scale gap is unmistakable: Broadcom books more AI semiconductor revenue in one quarter than Marvell targets from custom silicon in all of fiscal 2029. The dollar-yen pair in Tokyo foreign exchange trading on the 6th is focused on the battle around the 158 level ahead of Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech scheduled for the afternoon. In overseas markets the previous day, the pair briefly rose to 158.30, but struggled to extend gains as the rise in U.S. long-term yields paused, closing in the upper 157 range. The market remains on edge as participants try to gauge how far the governor will delve into monetary policy in his address at the National Securities Convention.
In New York trading on the 5th, dollar-yen retreated from domestic yen-buyback speculation following a Bloomberg report that the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) did not discuss a basic portfolio review at its September meeting. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield briefly climbed to around 5.3472%, its highest level in roughly 24 years since 2002, strengthening dollar buying on widening Japan-U.S. interest rate differentials and pushing the pair up to 158.30.
Additionally, concerns over France's fiscal deterioration and Spain's announcement of a snap general election (voting on November 29) drove euro weakness and dollar strength. The euro briefly fell to $1.1161 against the dollar, and the dollar index (DXY) against major currencies rose to 102.53, providing further support for dollar-yen. On the other hand, reports of increased crude oil exports from the Middle East led to lower oil prices, which helped stem the yen's decline.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, in her policy speech on the 5th, explained her economic policy: "Through responsible active fiscal policy, we will draw out domestic investment, raise Japan's potential growth rate, increase quality employment and income, improve consumer sentiment, boost business earnings, and achieve a virtuous cycle under GDP expansion where tax revenues naturally increase."
Regarding funding sources for consumption tax cuts, she stated she would "secure them without relying on special deficit-financing bonds so as to earn market confidence," adding that the government would "appropriately control government bond issuance while taking into account the effects of economic growth" and "nimbly take necessary measures if the market shows unexpected movements." The remarks appeared to foreground concerns about the yen's depreciation and rising interest rates since the administration took office, and were interpreted as a factor restraining yen weakness.
Mixed Expectations Ahead of Governor Ueda's Speech
Today's biggest focus is Governor Ueda's speech at the National Securities Convention, scheduled for 3:35 p.m. The governor and BOJ policy board members have tended, during previous rate hike phases, to send messages on wage trends and the functioning of the government bond market through speeches ahead of monetary policy meetings.
At its September 17-18 monetary policy meeting, the BOJ raised its policy rate from 1.00% to 1.25%. The vote was 7 in favor and 2 against, bringing rates to their highest level in 31 years since April 1995. The hike came just three months after the June meeting — the shortest interval since the BOJ ended negative interest rates in March 2024. In September, the ECB (on the 10th) and the Fed (on the 16th) also moved to hike rates, marking the first time since 2006 — 20 years — that Japan, the U.S., and Europe all raised rates simultaneously.

The market prices only about a 24% probability of an additional rate hike at the October 29-30 meeting, while an additional hike at the December meeting (17th-18th) is almost fully priced in. From October, government subsidies for electricity and gas bills will end, with October usage charges for the 10 major power companies rising by roughly 800 to 1,600 yen compared to September usage. With inflation expected to rise, some market participants are wary of consecutive rate hikes. The governor stated at his post-meeting press conference in September that "a change in the policy phase" was behind the "acceleration in the pace of rate hikes." Attention is on whether he will reference a hike at the October or December meeting in today's speech, or limit his remarks to industry-wide topics.
On the hawkish side, Tokyo's September core CPI rose 2.7% year-on-year, and August core CPI excluding special factors rose 2.6% year-on-year, indicating persistent inflationary pressure. On the dovish side, the governor recently stated that "large rate hikes or consecutive hikes multiple times would depend on whether there is a high risk that prices will rise dramatically beyond the target, or whether they have already exceeded the target," signaling a cautious view on consecutive hikes.
Therefore, in today's speech, what matters is not only whether he references additional rate hikes themselves, but also how far he goes in assessing inflation and discussing the future pace of hikes. If the governor makes remarks suggesting an early additional hike or an acceleration in the pace of hikes, yen buying is likely to strengthen. Conversely, if he maintains his cautious stance, dollar buying on Japan-U.S. interest rate differentials could re-intensify.

U.S. Data and Fed Officials' Remarks Also in Focus
The U.S. September ISM Non-Manufacturing Index released on the 5th came in at 54.9, slightly below market expectations (55.0) and down from the previous month (55.4). However, it remained above the 50.0 threshold separating expansion from contraction for the 27th consecutive month. Among major components, prices paid rose to 74.0, the highest level in four years and two months, indicating strong inflationary pressure. Employment also rose to 50.1, while new orders declined to 59.8.
New York Fed President Williams is scheduled to speak during New York hours, but he has already expressed a negative view on consecutive rate hikes this month, and the prevailing market view is that a surprise is unlikely. In Europe, a speech by Bank of England MPC member Mann, eurozone August retail sales, and a speech by ECB Executive Board member Cipollone are scheduled. articles.title: Korea Redesignates 92 Districts as Population-Declining Areas - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korea Redesignates 92 Districts as Population-Declining Areas  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
The government has redrawn its list of population-declining areas for the first time in five years, adding Busan's Geumjeong District, Dongducheon in Gyeonggi Province and Tongyeong in South Gyeongsang Province. Busan's Dong District, Daegu's Seo District and Yeonggwang County in Jeonnam were removed after their demographic conditions improved. The government will also overhaul the 1 trillion won annual regional extinction response fund, shifting it away from building facilities toward projects that improve housing, income and care services and encourage people to settle in these areas.
The Ministry of the Interior and Safety said on the 7th that it has redesignated 92 cities, counties and districts nationwide as population-declining areas after a comprehensive analysis of population size, demographic structure and regional vitality, the first review since the initial designation five years ago. Eighteen areas were placed on the watchlist for population decline. Compared with the first designation in 2021, the number of population-declining areas rose by three from 89, while the watchlist count was unchanged.
In this review, Busan's Geumjeong District, Dongducheon and Tongyeong moved up from the watchlist to full designation as population-declining areas. Busan's Buk District and Yecheon and Chilgok counties in North Gyeongsang Province were newly added to the watchlist, keeping the total at 18.
Busan's Dong District, Daegu's Seo District and Yeonggwang County, which dropped off the list after demographic conditions and regional vitality improved, will be classified under a newly created "population vitality plus" category. Gyeongju in North Gyeongsang Province and Gangneung, Sokcho and Inje County in Gangwon State, which were removed from the watchlist, will receive the same support. The ministry decided to maintain existing support for these areas for the next five years to prevent their recovery from stalling if assistance were cut off immediately upon removal.
The government also revised its selection criteria to better reflect actual conditions on the ground. In addition to the existing indicators — average annual rate of population change, the shares of older adults and children, the crude birth rate, net youth migration and fiscal self-reliance — the ministry added the share of urbanized land, the number of employed people and the de facto population, producing a nine-indicator "population vitality index." The aim is to capture not only changes in registered residents but also the people who actually work and live in each area, as well as economic vitality.
The support framework for population-declining areas will change as well. The 1 trillion won annual regional extinction response fund will move away from simply expanding facilities and instead be allocated to projects that link facilities with programming to generate real local activity and settlement. Investment will expand in projects that improve living conditions such as housing, income and care services and strengthen local self-sufficiency. For challenges that individual cities and counties cannot resolve alone, the ministry will strengthen cooperation at the level of broader living zones, bringing together neighboring areas, provincial governments and the central government.
Performance management of the fund will also be tightened. The ministry plans to systematically track whether spending translates into actual changes in population and residents' daily lives, and to direct more support to areas that deliver stronger results. Population-declining areas currently receive 44 administrative and fiscal exceptions as well as tax benefits, including preferential taxation on second homes outside the capital region, expanded acquisition tax cuts for first-time home purchases by young adults, and eased employment and residency requirements for foreign nationals. The government plans to identify additional exceptions that local residents and businesses can feel directly.
The government assessed that some indicators have improved since population-declining areas were first designated in 2021. The population of these areas fell 6.0% between 2018 and 2021, but the decline narrowed to 4.3% from 2022 to 2025. Migration also turned around, from an average net outflow of 32,251 people a year in 2020 and 2021 to an average net inflow of 1,615 a year from 2022 to 2025.
Still, the national population continues to shrink and concentration in the capital region persists. South Korea's total population peaked at 51.84 million in 2020 and fell to 51.68 million last year. Over the same period, the capital region's share of the population rose to 51.0% last year from 49.9% in 2019. The ministry said low birth rates and population aging, combined with concentration in the capital region, are making it harder for local areas to sustain transportation, commercial districts and services such as health care, education and child care, which in turn drives more young adults away in a vicious cycle.
Interior Minister Yoon Ho-jung said the redesignation "more accurately reflects how population and local conditions have changed over the past five years, and complements the system so that areas whose conditions have improved can maintain continuity in policy support." He added, "We will concentrate government-wide support tailored to local conditions in population-declining areas, and for population vitality plus areas, we will make sure the recovery they worked so hard to achieve is not cut short."

articles.title: Chip Veterans Who Left for China Found Few Stayed Long at CXMT - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Chip Veterans Who Left for China Found Few Stayed Long at CXMT  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Twenty-seven veteran semiconductor engineers from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix moved to Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) after averaging more than 15 years at the Korean chipmakers, according to a lawmaker's review of public career records. Their average tenure at CXMT was just 2.9 years, and 26 of the 27 have already left the company.
The office of Rep. Choi Soo-jin of the People Power Party, a member of the National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee, said on the 6th that it had reviewed LinkedIn and other global business platform profiles and counted 27 senior technical staff who joined CXMT — 23 from Samsung Electronics and four from SK hynix.
Their combined service at the Korean conglomerates totaled 415.9 years, or an average of 15.4 years each. Six were principal engineers or executives with more than 20 years in mass-production operations.
Their specialties varied: eight in circuit design, seven in process integration, four in unit processes and equipment, four in yield and defect analysis, and two in advanced packaging. More recently, the review found, engineers working on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) design and advanced packaging — not just commodity DRAM — have also moved to CXMT.
Fifteen of the group joined CXMT only after passing through equipment and materials suppliers, foreign-invested companies or universities following their departure from Samsung Electronics or SK hynix. The lawmaker's office said this pattern suggested "stepping-stone" job moves designed to get around non-compete agreements, which typically run one to two years.
The terms offered by the Chinese side were striking. Headhunter proposals obtained by the office included pay increases of 60% to double existing salaries, employment guarantees of three to five years, and support for rental housing and children's education costs.
CXMT's research and development workforce grew about 2.9-fold, from 2,606 at the end of 2022 to 7,491 in June this year. Of the 27 who moved from Korea, however, only one remains at CXMT, with average tenure at 2.9 years. Seven of those who left went on to other Chinese chip companies, including Huawei's Hong Kong research center and HiSilicon.
The office said CXMT may have drawn intensively on the Korean engineers' experience while building plants and stabilizing production processes. Public career records alone, however, do not confirm why individuals left or whether technology was actually transferred.
"Semiconductor technology is not just blueprints. It is the experience and know-how that people accumulate over 20 to 30 years," Choi said. "We need to build a national tracking system to identify and manage the movement of core personnel, and we need bold compensation and re-employment incentives so that talent can put its capabilities to work at home."
Separately, nearly half of Korea's science and engineering workforce is considering a move abroad within three years. In a Bank of Korea survey last year of 2,694 researchers with master's or doctoral degrees — 1,916 based in Korea and 778 overseas — 42.9% of those working in Korea said they were considering taking a job abroad within three years.
Those in their 20s and 30s accounted for 70% of that group. The most frequently cited reason was financial, such as salary, at 66.7%. On average, researchers working overseas earned about twice as much as those in Korea. Non-financial factors also ranked high, including the research ecosystem and professional networks at 61.1% and assurance of career opportunities at 48.8%.

articles.title: Once the buyer, now the suitor: AMDs Lisa Su due back in Korea - Aju Press
articles.summary: Once the buyer, now the suitor: AMDs Lisa Su due back in Korea  Aju Press
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, October 06 (AJP) - For decades, the semiconductor industry’s pecking order was relatively straightforward: chip designers and system companies called the shots, while memory makers competed to supply them.
The artificial intelligence boom is starting to turn that relationship on its head.
AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su is due in South Korea this week, seven months after her previous visit in March, as the U.S. chipmaker seeks the advanced memory and manufacturing partnerships needed to challenge Nvidia in AI computing.
Su will attend AMD Gamer Day 2026 in Seoul on Wednesday alongside Jack Huynh, senior vice president and general manager of AMD’s Computing and Graphics Group. A media Q&A is scheduled for the same day, while meetings with Korean AI chip companies and government officials are expected during the trip.
Behind the gaming event lies a much bigger semiconductor story.
As AI accelerators become more powerful, access to high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, increasingly determines how quickly chip designers can turn their ambitions into products.
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix together accounted for more than 80 percent of global HBM revenue in the second quarter, according to Counterpoint Research figures. That concentration gives the Korean suppliers considerable leverage over the companies competing to build the next generation of AI systems.
“The relationship between the buyer and supplier has changed significantly,” said Kim Deok-kee, a professor of electronic engineering at Sejong University.
“In the past, memory companies were largely in the weaker position,” Kim said. “Now memory has become so critical that you could almost say the memory companies have become the ones holding the upper hand.”
For AMD, the stakes are particularly high.
Its Instinct graphics processors are central to its effort to narrow Nvidia’s commanding lead in AI accelerators. But that requires more than designing faster chips. The processors need increasingly large amounts of advanced memory to deliver data to their computing cores at high speed.
Securing HBM has consequently become a strategic priority.
“The first priority is securing memory,” Kim said. “More than future technology itself, securing allocations of the highest-performance and most expensive HBM is likely the immediate priority.”
There is an irony to AMD’s position: it helped pioneer the technology it now needs to secure.
SK hynix announced the development of its first HBM product using through-silicon vias — vertical connections between stacked memory chips — in December 2013, following joint development with AMD. AMD brought first-generation HBM to its Fiji-based graphics products in 2015, well before the generative AI boom made the technology indispensable to advanced accelerators.
What began as an architectural innovation has become a scarce component sought by the world’s leading AI chipmakers.
Samsung is emerging as an especially important partner in AMD’s response.
During Su’s March visit, she traveled to Samsung’s semiconductor complex in Pyeongtaek and signed a memorandum of understanding with Vice Chairman and CEO Jun Young-hyun to expand cooperation in AI memory and computing.
The agreement covers primary HBM4 supply for AMD’s next-generation Instinct MI455X accelerator, alongside advanced DDR5 memory for sixth-generation EPYC server processors and systems built around AMD’s Helios rack-scale platform.
It builds on Samsung’s existing role as AMD’s primary HBM3E partner for the MI350X and MI355X accelerators.
The relationship could extend beyond memory.
Samsung and AMD also agreed to discuss a potential foundry partnership under which Samsung would manufacture future AMD products. Such an arrangement could broaden their cooperation across memory, chip production and advanced packaging, although a manufacturing agreement has not been announced.
For Su, those discussions draw on relationships that predate her AMD career.
She spent more than a decade at IBM, holding senior positions in semiconductor technology development and manufacturing.
“Su had experience working with Samsung Foundry around 2005 while she was at IBM, so she likely still knows people within Samsung’s foundry business,” said an industry source who worked with her at the time.
Su became vice president of IBM’s Semiconductor Research and Development Center in 2005. By 2006, she was heading a joint development alliance involving IBM, Samsung, Chartered Semiconductor and Infineon that worked on advanced manufacturing processes.
“Su understands not only software and system architecture but semiconductor devices and manufacturing as well,” the source said. “She understands how foundries operate.”
That background could become increasingly relevant as AMD explores cooperation extending from memory supply to manufacturing and packaging.
Su’s return does not establish that another supply deal is imminent. It does, however, come as AMD’s competitive ambitions depend increasingly on technologies concentrated in South Korea.
The country’s role in that strategy has evolved. AMD’s work with SK hynix helped establish HBM’s first generation; its expanding Samsung partnership now reaches into HBM4 and potentially contract chipmaking.
For Korean memory makers, the change is significant. Their products are becoming a constraint around which even the most powerful chip designers must plan.
Nvidia and AMD still wield enormous influence over the AI industry. But without sufficient advanced memory, neither can deliver its fastest processors at the scale customers demand.
That gives Korean suppliers greater bargaining power — and Su a compelling reason to keep returning.
“Securing memory comes first,” Kim said. “After that, there is the question of jointly developing the next technologies — memory, foundry and the overall architecture.”
For AMD, both increasingly lead to South Korea.

President Donald Trump’s 100% tariff on certain patented pharmaceutical products took effect for covered drugmakers on Sept. 29, raising questions about the potential impacts on drug prices, domestic manufacturing and smaller pharmaceutical companies.
The tariff was imposed under Section 232 and applies to patented pharmaceutical products and associated ingredients unless they qualify for specific exemptions or alternative tariff arrangements. The White House said that the measure is intended to strengthen U.S. pharmaceutical supply chains and encourage companies to expand domestic production.
However, the actual impacts are likely to vary considerably for drugmakers because the policy includes several exemptions. Companies that combine qualifying onshoring commitments with Most Favored Nation (“MFN”) pricing agreements can receive a zero tariff through Jan. 20, 2029.
Specialty Medicines Receive Protection
The new rules provide zero-tariff treatment for certain specialty medicines, subject to eligibility requirements. These include orphan drugs, nuclear medicines, plasma-derived therapies, fertility treatments, cell and gene therapies, antibody-drug conjugates, and medical countermeasures. Animal-health pharmaceuticals are also covered under the specialty-product provisions.
Trade arrangements reduce the tariff burden for several major pharmaceutical-producing markets. The proclamation sets a 15% rate for covered products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, while companies that commit to expanding their U.S. production will be subject to a 20% tariff, per CNN Business.
This means that the headline 100% tariff will not apply uniformly across the pharmaceutical industry.
Generic Drugs Are Excluded From This Tariff Structure
One of the most important distinctions is between patented and generic medicines.
The administration has specifically decided not to impose Section 232 tariffs on generic pharmaceuticals, biosimilars and their associated ingredients at this time. The policy will be reviewed as the government continues monitoring pharmaceutical imports.
Consequently, the immediate tariff exposure is concentrated in patented and innovative medicines rather than the broader pharmaceutical market.
Small to Mid-Sized Drugmakers Face Different Challenges
The policy could, nevertheless, put greater pressure on smaller and mid-sized drugmakers that depend on overseas manufacturing or contract manufacturers.
A major concern is that companies with fewer financial resources may find it more difficult to quickly establish U.S. manufacturing capacity. Higher production costs, especially for those that depend more heavily on external suppliers, could affect margins, pricing decisions, and investment in research and development.
Building a manufacturing facility is also a long-term process that requires substantial capital investment, regulatory approvals and specialized infrastructure. As a result, smaller companies may have difficulty responding quickly if their products fall outside the available exemptions.
Pharma ETFs in Focus
The next phase of the tariff story will depend heavily on how drugmakers respond. Companies could increase U.S. production, renegotiate supply chains or seek tariff relief under the available exemptions and agreements.
For pharmaceutical ETFs, investors may therefore want to monitor domestic manufacturing commitments, exposure to imported patented drugs and ingredients, product exemptions, and company-specific MFN agreements.
The policy creates a potentially important divide within the pharmaceutical sector: companies with established U.S. manufacturing or qualifying agreements may face a different cost structure from smaller drugmakers that rely more heavily on overseas or contract production.

articles.title: US Secretary of State Rubio says the era of free trade agreements is unlikely to return for the foreseeable future - Newsquawk
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Rubio says the era of free trade agreements is unlikely to return for the foreseeable future  Newsquawk
articles.full_text:
Context
Formal trade liberalisation has been in retreat across successive US administrations of both parties, and remarks of this kind from a sitting Secretary of State tend to confirm an existing posture rather than create a new one; the shift from multilateral tariff reduction toward managed trade, industrial policy, and security-screened supply chains has been the direction of travel through multiple administrations. The transmission is structural rather than a one-day repricing: a durable absence of new FTAs keeps tariff uncertainty elevated, sustains reshoring and friend-shoring capex, and entrenches the margin advantage of domestic producers in protected sectors over import-exposed peers. The distinction worth drawing is between rhetoric and instrument: statements alone do not change schedules, but they shape the negotiating baseline for bilateral deals, which historically get re-badged as narrower sectoral or critical-minerals arrangements rather than comprehensive agreements. Actors with prior form on protectionist trade policy have tended to pair such language with targeted levies or quotas, so the follow-ons are actual tariff actions, exclusions processes, and any parallel remarks from the trade representative's office. Retaliation risk from partners is the established second-round pattern in episodes of this kind. As a policy signal rather than an action, the note carries direction but no immediate mechanical trigger.

articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- USD/JPY traded near 157.90 in Asian hours on Tuesday after modest gains in the prior session, with the pair locked in a tight range.
- Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi advanced expansionary measures, including a cut to the consumption tax on food, while pledging no additional bond issuance.
- Bank of Japan commentary kept the door open for another rate hike this year, as inflation concerns persist above the 2% target and policy timing remains uncertain.
Fiscal Support in Japan Calms Market Concerns
USD/JPY showed limited movement during Asian trading on Tuesday, hovering around 157.90 after recording only small gains in the previous session. The pair has settled into a constrained trading band as investors react to recent Japanese fiscal developments.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been pressing ahead with expansionary economic policies despite ongoing worries about the softness of the Yen and the level of public debt. In a parliamentary speech, Takaichi committed to reducing the consumption tax on food items, while also emphasizing that the government plans to obtain the required financing without resorting to fresh bond issuance, a move intended to reassure financial markets about fiscal discipline.
BOJ Rate Path Clouded by Inflation Risks
Uncertainty over the Bank of Japan’s next steps in monetary policy continues to weigh on sentiment. A summary of views from the central bank’s September meeting pointed to mounting concern that inflation could run above the 2% objective, leaving the possibility of another interest rate increase within the current year very much alive.
Even so, with policy meetings scheduled for October and December, the Bank of Japan offered little guidance on when any potential rate move might occur. This lack of specificity has kept investors guessing on the pace and timing of any further normalization.
Geopolitical Tensions Support Safe-Haven Dollar Demand
Looking ahead, the US Dollar may find additional support against the Yen as safe-haven flows build amid rising geopolitical risk. Citing Xinhua News Agency, the report noted that Yemen’s Houthi group claimed responsibility for coordinated drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabian military sites, an oil facility, and key airports.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said a successful strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh disrupted local air traffic, introducing new turbulence into global markets and potentially reinforcing demand for the Greenback as a perceived refuge in times of stress.
HSBC Sees Profit-Driven Forces Behind US Inflation
Strategists at HSBC focused on the composition of US inflation, challenging the narrative that it is primarily a function of “surging oil and computing costs, as well as the lingering impact of tariffs.” They examined the gross value-added deflator, described as a gauge that tracks “inflation generated by profits, wages, and non-labour related costs.”
According to their assessment, this framework indicates that the recent pickup in headline inflation “appears to have been driven mainly by stronger profit growth,” rather than solely by higher input costs.

Korea Stock Market (KRX) Today (October 06): South Korea's stock market returned from its extended holiday break with a striking split on Tuesday, October 6. The KOSPI started the session on a positive note after overnight gains on Wall Street but lost momentum as investors locked in profits in major technology stocks and remained cautious about elevated bond yields. At the same time, the smaller KOSDAQ attracted strong buying, particularly in cybersecurity, semiconductor equipment and other growth stocks.
The contrast showed how investors were moving money away from expensive large-cap chip names while chasing companies tied to emerging technology themes.
The KOSPI eventually finished lower, while the KOSDAQ extended its rally. Rising global yields, a weaker won, foreign selling and caution ahead of corporate earnings weighed on the mainboard. Meanwhile, recent financial-sector hacking incidents sparked a powerful rally in cybersecurity stocks on the KOSDAQ.
The main reason behind the KOSPI decline was a combination of profit-taking in semiconductor stocks, foreign selling and concerns about elevated global bond yields.
The benchmark initially benefited from gains on Wall Street. The KOSPI opened at 7,044.67, up 0.58%, after the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.05% in the previous session. However, the early optimism faded as investors focused on rising Treasury yields and upcoming corporate earnings.
Technology stocks became the biggest drag. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix both declined as investors reduced exposure to chipmakers ahead of earnings updates.
Higher borrowing costs also continued to weigh on sentiment. U.S. Treasury yields were trading around multidecade highs, while the Korean won weakened against the U.S. dollar. Yonhap reported that the won was around 1,344 won per dollar by late morning.
Foreign investors also remained cautious. Earlier in the session, foreigners were already net sellers of Korean shares, adding to pressure on the KOSPI.
The KOSPI erased its early gains and moved decisively lower during Tuesday's session.
The index opened at 7,044.67, up 0.58%, but fell below the psychologically important 7,000 mark as selling intensified. By late morning, it stood at 6,964.85, down 0.56%.
The final session data supplied for October 6 shows the KOSPI closing at 6,923.68, down 80.06 points or 1.14%.
The reversal was important because it showed that investors were unwilling to chase the market higher after the holiday break. Instead, they used the early strength to take profits, particularly in heavily weighted semiconductor companies.

The KOSDAQ's rise was closely linked to strong demand for cybersecurity stocks after a series of financial-sector hacking incidents raised expectations for greater spending on digital security.
Genians, SANDS Lab, AhnLab, RaonSecure and other security companies recorded major gains during the session. Yonhap reported that Genians, AhnLab and RaonSecure were among the strongest movers in morning trading, with some stocks temporarily reaching their daily upper limits.

The decline came as investors reassessed their positions before the company's upcoming preliminary third-quarter earnings guidance. The market is closely watching Samsung's semiconductor performance, particularly high-bandwidth memory and AI-related demand.

articles.title: Samsung earnings kick off key October for chip industry - Aju Press
articles.summary: Samsung earnings kick off key October for chip industry  Aju Press
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, October 05 (AJP) - The global semiconductor industry is heading into a busy stretch of October, with Samsung Electronics set to report preliminary earnings this week before a series of major chip events and earnings releases put the strength of the AI-driven boom to another test.
Samsung is scheduled to release its preliminary third-quarter results on Thursday, Oct. 8, providing the first major earnings signal from South Korea's semiconductor industry after Micron Technology delivered record results and a bullish outlook last week.
Micron forecast even tighter memory supply conditions in 2027 and 2028, driven by continued demand for high-bandwidth memory and other chips used in AI infrastructure. Its outlook helped reinforce expectations that the current memory upcycle could extend well beyond this year.
Attention will then shift to a series of industry events and earnings releases next week.
Samsung Semiconductor will participate in the OCP Global Summit in San Jose from Oct. 12 to 15, where it plans to showcase memory and storage technologies designed for expanding AI infrastructure, including CXL-based memory pooling and technologies for AI inference.
In Seoul, SEDEX 2026, South Korea's largest semiconductor exhibition, will run from Oct. 14 to 16 at COEX, bringing together Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and companies across the chip equipment, materials and component supply chain. The event will include sessions on advanced semiconductor packaging and other next-generation technologies.
The focus will also turn to global semiconductor bellwethers, with ASML and TSMC expected to report third-quarter results in mid-October.
Their results will provide further clues on whether strong AI-related spending is continuing to translate into demand for advanced chipmaking equipment and leading-edge semiconductor production.
The busy calendar follows Micron's stronger-than-expected outlook and South Korea's record semiconductor exports in September, which more than tripled from a year earlier amid surging AI demand.
For investors and the chip industry, Samsung's preliminary results this week will mark the next major checkpoint in determining how much momentum the AI-driven memory boom carries into the final quarter of the year.
